Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

LONDON, England (CNN)  -- Guantanamo Bay's legacy of torture will hurt the United States even if President Obama makes good on a pledge to close the prison camp, a former inmate says. Moazzam Begg says that during intense interrogations at Guantanamo Bay, he would have confessed to anything. Justice will be impossible to mete out to the alleged terrorists and war criminals held there because any confessions must be tainted by the methods used to obtain them, ex-prisoner Moazzam Begg told CNN. Begg says he would have confessed to anything during interrogations while he was held at Guantanamo for nearly three years. "What procedure can you use on people who have been systematically tortured including waterboarding, including being stripped naked and beaten? What sort of evidence can be admitted into a court of law that has been extracted under that process?" asked Begg.  Watch what Begg thinks of Guantanamo » . The new administration  has said that waterboarding, which causes the feeling of drowning, is torture. Begg, who is British, was captured during the war in Afghanistan and accused of aiding the Taliban regime.  His family has always maintained he was a victim of mistaken identity. He was sent back to his home in Britain by the Bush administration in 2005 and never prosecuted. President Obama on Wednesday moved closer to making good on his campaign promise. The administration is drafting executive orders calling for the detention facility's closure, officials said. Earlier in the day, a judge granted Obama's request for a 120-day suspension of prosecutions so a review of all cases of suspected terrorists could take place. During his inaugural speech, he stressed that ideals of justice did not need to be thrown out to ensure the nation's safety. "Our Founding Fathers, faced with perils we can scarcely imagine, drafted a charter to assure the rule of law and the rights of man, a charter expanded by the blood of generations. Those ideals still light the world, and we will not give them up for expedience's sake," Obama said.  Watch what could be next for Guantanamo » . Legal issues are already complicating the cases of some of the most important terror suspects, like Mohamed al-Qahtani, the so-called 20th hijacker, who has been accused of helping to plan and possibly participate in the September 11, 2001, terrorist attacks. Earlier this month, the retired judge in charge of determining which Guantanamo detainees should be tried by a U.S. military commission told The Washington Post that al-Qahtani was tortured and therefore could not  be put forward for prosecution. "Guantanamo Bay is the most notorious prison on earth," Begg said. He said he believes Guantanamo is a radicalizing force for militants around the world. Looking beyond high-profile suspects, human rights campaigners say there is little evidence to prosecute dozens of Guantanamo inmates still being held. They argue that keeping those detainees locked up will not help keep al Qaeda at bay. "I think it's actually one of the most harmful myths about it, that we can't let people go because we've got the tiger by the tail," said Cori Crider of the human rights organization Reprieve. Chris Arendt, a former guard at Guantanamo Bay, says the Obama administration must rethink and reform the way it detains and prosecutes future terror suspects -- and do more than just close Guantanamo. "We're focused on this one camp that has become the star of the whole show. But there are camps everywhere," he said. "There are camps in Iraq, in Afghanistan -- every country that American or the coalition forces have set their feet. None of those detainees are seeing any justice."

outputs.L1:
**LONDON, England (CNN) —** Guantanamo Bay’s legacy of torture will continue to damage the United States even if President Obama fulfills his pledge to close the prison camp, according to a former detainee.

Moazzam Begg, who was held at Guantanamo for nearly three years, said he would have confessed to anything during the intense interrogations he endured. He told CNN that it would be impossible to administer justice to the alleged terrorists and war criminals detained there because any confessions would inevitably be tainted by the methods used to obtain them.

“What procedure can you use on people who have been systematically tortured, including waterboarding, including being stripped naked and beaten? What sort of evidence can be admitted into a court of law that has been extracted under that process?” Begg asked.

*Watch what Begg thinks of Guantanamo »*

The new administration has said that waterboarding, which creates the sensation of drowning, constitutes torture.

Begg, a British citizen, was captured during the war in Afghanistan and accused of aiding the Taliban regime. His family has always maintained that he was a victim of mistaken identity. In 2005, the Bush administration returned him to his home in Britain, and he was never prosecuted.

On Wednesday, President Obama moved closer to fulfilling his campaign promise. Administration officials said executive orders calling for the detention facility’s closure were being drafted.

Earlier that day, a judge granted Obama’s request for a 120-day suspension of prosecutions to allow for a review of all cases involving suspected terrorists.

During his inaugural address, Obama emphasized that the nation did not need to abandon its ideals of justice to ensure its safety.

“Our Founding Fathers, faced with perils we can scarcely imagine, drafted a charter to assure the rule of law and the rights of man, a charter expanded by the blood of generations. Those ideals still light the world, and we will not give them up for expedience’s sake,” Obama said.

*Watch what could be next for Guantanamo »*

Legal issues are already complicating the cases of some of the most significant terror suspects, including Mohamed al-Qahtani, the so-called 20th hijacker, who has been accused of helping to plan and possibly participate in the September 11, 2001, terrorist attacks.

Earlier this month, the retired judge responsible for determining which Guantanamo detainees should be tried by a U.S. military commission told *The Washington Post* that al-Qahtani had been tortured and therefore could not be put forward for prosecution.

“Guantanamo Bay is the most notorious prison on Earth,” Begg said. He added that he believes the facility serves as a radicalizing force for militants around the world.

Beyond the high-profile suspects, human rights campaigners say there is little evidence with which to prosecute dozens of detainees who remain at Guantanamo. They argue that continuing to imprison those detainees will not help keep al Qaeda at bay.

“I think it’s actually one of the most harmful myths about it, that we can’t let people go because we’ve got the tiger by the tail,” said Cori Crider of the human rights organization Reprieve.

Chris Arendt, a former guard at Guantanamo Bay, said the Obama administration must rethink and reform how it detains and prosecutes future terror suspects—and do more than simply close Guantanamo.

“We’re focused on this one camp that has become the star of the whole show. But there are camps everywhere,” he said. “There are camps in Iraq, in Afghanistan—every country that American or the coalition forces have set their feet. None of those detainees are seeing any justice.”
outputs.L2:
**LONDON, England (CNN) —** A former Guantanamo Bay detainee says the prison’s record of torture will continue to damage the United States even if President Obama fulfills his promise to shut it down.

Moazzam Begg told CNN that the harsh interrogation techniques used at the facility have compromised any admissions made by prisoners, making it impossible to fairly administer justice to those accused of terrorism and war crimes. Begg, who spent almost three years at Guantanamo, said the pressure was so severe that he would have admitted to anything.

He questioned how courts could handle cases involving prisoners who had been subjected to systematic abuse, including waterboarding, forced nudity and beatings. Begg asked what evidence obtained through such treatment could legitimately be accepted in a court.

The new administration has classified waterboarding—a technique that creates the sensation of drowning—as torture.

Begg, a British citizen, was detained during the Afghanistan war and accused of supporting the Taliban government. His family has consistently argued that authorities had mistaken him for someone else. In 2005, the Bush administration returned him to Britain, where he was never charged or tried.

On Wednesday, Obama took another step toward carrying out his campaign commitment to close Guantanamo. Officials said the administration was preparing executive orders directing that the detention center be shut down.

Earlier that day, a judge approved Obama’s request to pause prosecutions for 120 days, allowing the administration to examine every case involving suspected terrorists.

In his inaugural address, Obama argued that protecting the country did not require abandoning principles of justice. He said the Founding Fathers had created a framework guaranteeing the rule of law and human rights despite confronting dangers that are difficult to imagine today. Those values, strengthened through the sacrifices of later generations, remained an example to the world and should not be surrendered simply for convenience, he said.

Legal complications have already affected proceedings against prominent terrorism suspects. One example is Mohamed al-Qahtani, described as the alleged “20th hijacker,” who has been accused of helping organize—and perhaps intending to take part in—the September 11, 2001, attacks.

Earlier in the month, the retired judge responsible for deciding which Guantanamo prisoners should face U.S. military commissions told *The Washington Post* that al-Qahtani had been tortured and therefore could not be recommended for prosecution.

Begg described Guantanamo Bay as the world’s most infamous prison and said he believes it encourages radicalization among militants internationally.

Beyond the best-known detainees, human rights advocates say prosecutors have little evidence against dozens of prisoners who remain at the facility. They also reject the argument that continuing to imprison those men is necessary to contain al Qaeda.

Cori Crider of the human rights group Reprieve said one of the most damaging misconceptions is the belief that the United States cannot release detainees because doing so would mean losing control of a dangerous situation.

Former Guantanamo guard Chris Arendt said Obama’s administration must go further than closing that single prison. In his view, it also needs to reconsider and overhaul how future terrorism suspects are detained and prosecuted.

Arendt said attention has centered on Guantanamo because it has become the most visible symbol of the detention system. However, he noted that similar camps exist in Iraq, Afghanistan and every country where U.S. or coalition troops have established a presence. He said detainees at those locations are not receiving justice either.
outputs.L3:
Former Guantanamo Bay detainee Moazzam Begg warned that the prison’s legacy of torture and abusive interrogation would continue to damage the United States even if the detention facility were closed. He argued that allegations of mistreatment had undermined the credibility of the justice process and harmed America’s international reputation.

According to Begg, confessions obtained through waterboarding, beatings, and other coercive methods were inherently tainted and could not be considered reliable evidence in court. The use of such techniques, he said, made it difficult to determine whether detainees’ statements were truthful or simply made to end their suffering.

Begg, a British citizen who was accused of aiding the Taliban, spent nearly three years in detention, including time at Guantanamo. He was released without prosecution in 2005 and returned to the United Kingdom.

After taking office, President Barack Obama’s administration began preparing orders to close Guantanamo and obtained a 120-day suspension of prosecutions so officials could review detainees’ cases. Obama maintained that the United States could protect its national security without abandoning the rule of law or its commitment to fundamental human rights.
outputs.L4:
Former Guantanamo detainee Moazzam Begg argued that the use of coercive interrogation techniques had contaminated much of the evidence gathered from prisoners at the detention facility. Drawing on his own experience in U.S. custody, Begg said methods such as waterboarding, prolonged isolation, sleep deprivation, threats, and physical abuse could compel detainees to say whatever interrogators wanted to hear. Statements obtained under such conditions, he maintained, could not be treated as reliable confessions.

That problem confronted the Obama administration as it reviewed detainees’ cases and prepared to close Guantanamo. Officials had to determine which prisoners could be released or transferred and which, if any, could be prosecuted. Yet evidence collected through abusive interrogations might be inadmissible in ordinary federal courts. Even when a detainee later repeated a confession under less coercive circumstances, prosecutors could face questions about whether the subsequent statement remained tainted by the original mistreatment.

Begg contended that torture did more than violate prisoners’ rights: it damaged the government’s ability to establish the truth. A detainee subjected to extreme pressure might provide false information, implicate innocent people, or invent details simply to end the suffering. Such claims could then enter intelligence files, shape later questioning, and become difficult to separate from independently verified evidence.

As a result, some detainees accused of serious crimes might never receive a credible trial. Releasing them could be politically controversial, while continuing to imprison them without charge would perpetuate the legal and moral failures associated with Guantanamo. Special military proceedings would not necessarily solve the problem, Begg suggested, because they too would struggle with evidence obtained through coercion and with doubts about fairness.

He therefore concluded that the consequences of Guantanamo would outlast the prison itself. Even if the facility closed, years of abusive interrogation and indefinite detention could continue to obstruct prosecutions, weaken confidence in American justice, and damage the United States’ international credibility. In Begg’s view, torture had not made justice easier to achieve; it may have made reliable justice impossible in some of the cases where it was needed most.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a news article on Obama’s planned closure of Guantanamo Bay, incorporating comments from former detainee Moazzam Begg, human-rights lawyer Cori Crider, and former guard Chris Arendt.
counterfactuals.output:
**Obama’s Guantanamo closure plan welcomed but campaigners demand accountability**

**WASHINGTON, Jan. 23, 2009** — President Barack Obama’s order to close the U.S. detention camp at Guantanamo Bay within a year has been welcomed by former prisoners, lawyers and some former military personnel, although human-rights advocates warned that shutting the prison would not by itself end the policies associated with it.

Obama signed an executive order Thursday directing officials to review the cases of roughly 245 detainees then held at the U.S. naval base in Cuba and to close the detention facility no later than January 2010. He also ordered an end to the CIA’s use of secret prisons and required interrogations to comply with rules set out in the Army Field Manual.

The move marked a sharp break with the Bush administration, which opened the Guantanamo prison in January 2002 to hold foreign terrorism suspects. Many detainees were confined for years without trial, while allegations of torture, coercive interrogation and other abuse damaged the United States’ standing abroad.

Moazzam Begg, a British citizen held at Guantanamo from 2003 until his release without charge in 2005, described the closure order as an important first step. Begg, who later campaigned on detainee issues, has said the government must also confront what happened to prisoners and provide due process rather than simply transferring them to other forms of indefinite detention.

Human-rights lawyer Cori Crider, who represented Guantanamo detainees through the legal organization Reprieve, similarly welcomed the deadline but cautioned that the details would determine whether the policy amounted to meaningful change. She argued that prisoners should either face fair trials in established courts or be released, and that detainees cleared to leave should not be returned to countries where they risk torture or persecution.

The administration faces difficult decisions over where to resettle prisoners who cannot safely return home, how to prosecute those accused of crimes and what to do in cases built partly on classified or coercively obtained evidence. Civil-liberties groups have urged Obama to reject proposals for a new system of preventive or indefinite detention on U.S. soil.

Chris Arendt, a former Guantanamo guard who later spoke publicly about the treatment of prisoners, said closing the camp was necessary but should be accompanied by an honest examination of conditions there. His accounts have highlighted the psychological pressure placed on both detainees and young guards, as well as the lasting consequences for those who served at the facility.

Republican critics warned that transferring detainees to the United States could create security risks and questioned whether other countries would accept released prisoners. Supporters of the order countered that federal courts and the regular military justice system were capable of handling terrorism cases.

Obama’s directive does not guarantee that every detainee will be freed or tried within the one-year period. It establishes an interagency review intended to determine which prisoners can be released, transferred or prosecuted.

For Begg, Crider and Arendt, however, the central test extends beyond the prison’s gates: whether the new administration ends indefinite detention and abuse, provides lawful proceedings and establishes accountability for the practices that made Guantanamo a global symbol of post-Sept. 11 excesses.
